issues.legal_issue: An appellate court reviewing an acquittal must leave it undisturbed when the trial court’s view is reasonably possible on the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after assessing the witnesses, documentary evidence, and defence evidence, and gave reasons for its conclusions.
The High Court reappraised the evidence, reversed the acquittal, and convicted the accused.
The Supreme Court found that the trial court’s conclusions were reasonably available on the evidence, even if another court might disagree with them.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have reversed the acquittal because the trial court’s view was a possible view; the acquittal was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an appellate court has full power to review and reappreciate the evidence in an appeal against acquittal. But the accused has a double presumption of innocence, and where two reasonable conclusions are possible, the acquittal should not be disturbed. The Court applied Sheo Swarup v. King Emperor, Tulsiram Kanu v. State, Balbir Singh v. State of Punjab, M.G. Agarwal v. State of Maharashtra, Khedu Mohton v. State of Bihar, Sambasivan v. State of Kerala, Bhagwan Singh v. State of M.P., State of Goa v. Sanjay Thakran, and Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka. It also noted the special statutory right of appeal under Section 379 of the Code and the distinction discussed in State of Rajasthan v. Abdul Mannan.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to reverse a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_acquitted: The trial court found the accused not guilty.
predicates.trial_view_reasonably_possible: The trial court’s view can reasonably be formed from the evidence and material on record.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal and the trial court’s evidence-based view is reasonably possible, the acquittal must not be reversed.

issues.legal_issue: The accused’s presence at the scene with weapons and their attack after a call, without further evidence of a prior agreement, does not establish criminal conspiracy.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses said to have knowledge of a prior plan denied that any agreement to commit murder had been made.
The trial court found that the prosecution had not proved a conspiracy, and the prosecutor had virtually conceded that the evidence did not establish the charge.
The High Court inferred a conspiracy from the accused arriving armed and attacking the deceased after a call from others.
The Supreme Court held that those circumstances, without further evidence, did not establish a prior arrangement or meeting of minds.
issues.conclusion: The charge of criminal conspiracy was not proved, and the trial court’s acquittal on that charge was a possible view that the High Court should not have displaced.
issues.legal_principle: Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code requires proof of an agreement or meeting of minds to commit an unlawful act. Because direct evidence of conspiracy is rarely available, it may be inferred from circumstances; however, presence at the scene with weapons and responding to a call, without further evidence, does not establish a prior agreement. The general restraint on reversing a possible acquittal also applies under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the principles in Sheo Swarup and Chandrappa.

predicates.alleged_conspirators_arrived_armed: The persons alleged to have conspired arrived at the scene carrying weapons.
predicates.attack_followed_a_call: The attack occurred after some persons called on others to attack.
predicates.evidence_of_prior_agreement_absent: There is no further evidence establishing a prior arrangement or meeting of minds to commit the offence.

issues.definition: When alleged conspirators arrive armed and attack after a call, but there is no evidence of prior agreement and the trial court acquitted them of conspiracy, the conspiracy is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must not displace a trial court’s acceptance of an alibi when the evidence reasonably supports the finding that the accused were elsewhere.
material_facts: The trial court accepted the alibi pleas of two accused on the basis of defence testimony and documents indicating their presence elsewhere at the time of the incident.
The High Court rejected those pleas, relying on gaps in the evidence about when one accused left an institution and the time of a document’s execution.
The Supreme Court found that the defence evidence and documents permitted the trial court’s view that the accused were not at the scene.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have rejected the trial court’s acceptance of the alibi pleas; the trial court’s view was a possible view.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the appellate court may review the evidence, but it must respect the trial court’s view where that view is reasonably possible. The Court applied the principles in Sheo Swarup and Chandrappa concerning the presumption of innocence and restraint in disturbing an acquittal.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to reverse a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_accepted_alibi: The trial court accepted a claim that the accused was elsewhere when the offence occurred.
predicates.evidence_reasonably_supports_presence_el: The defence evidence and documents reasonably support the finding that the accused was away from the scene.

issues.definition: When a trial court accepts an alibi on evidence that reasonably supports the accused being elsewhere, that finding must not be displaced in an appeal against acquittal.

issues.legal_issue: Convictions cannot stand where the evidence relied on to reverse an acquittal contains material weaknesses that leave the trial court’s reasonable doubt-based assessment as a possible view.
material_facts: The trial court found the principal eyewitness evidence unreliable or insufficient, noting improvements in testimony, uncertain identification, and the witnesses’ inability to identify specific attackers and acts.

Contemporaneous accounts differed materially: one report named no attackers, another named several, and the dying declaration named only a few; the dying declaration was interrupted when its maker became comatose.

The timing and contents of the first information report, the absence of injuries said to have resulted from stone pelting, and the failure of police witnesses to use their firearms raised further doubts.
The trial court also noted that the prosecution did not examine available independent witnesses and that the defence evidence placed some accused elsewhere.
The Supreme Court found the High Court’s conclusions on the evidence fragile and held that the trial court’s view was possible.
issues.conclusion: The convictions and sentences could not be sustained; the High Court’s judgment was set aside and the trial court’s acquittal was confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. In an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the appellate court may reappraise the evidence, but it must give due weight to the trial court’s credibility assessments and must not substitute its view where the acquittal reflects a reasonably possible conclusion. The Court applied Sheo Swarup and Chandrappa and considered the cumulative effect of the evidentiary inconsistencies and omissions.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to reverse a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_has_material_incons: The prosecution evidence contains material conflicts, omissions, or reliability problems concerning the occurrence or identification of the accused.
predicates.trial_court_found_reasonable_doubt: The trial court found that the prosecution evidence did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.acquittal_view_reasonably_possible: The trial court’s assessment of the evidence and resulting acquittal can reasonably be supported by the record.

issues.definition: When material weaknesses in the prosecution evidence support the trial court’s reasonable doubt and its acquittal is a possible view, convictions entered by reversing that acquittal cannot stand.
